# Mutant results — issue #22, realtime layer

<!-- Generated by `node mutants/run.mjs`. Do not edit by hand. -->

**94 run, 94 caught.**

Each row restores one earlier round‘s behaviour and reports which tests went red.
A `sql` mutant is applied to the live database and undone from the migration
file it names, because migrations are journalled and editing an applied one
changes nothing.

**Every artifact the suites consume is rebuilt** — `pnpm --filter "./packages/*"
build` runs before the baseline, and again around any mutation of a file under
`packages/`, because `packages/ingest` and `apps/server` resolve `@atrium/core`
and `@atrium/db` through their built `dist`. A ledger that skips this measures
whatever was on disk (#26 r6).

**The `detail` column counts the tests each mutant *claimed*, and only those.**
It used to be the total that failed, which is not byte-reproducible: the total
includes collateral — tests that fail for the same reason without being the pin —
and it moves whenever a suite gains a case. The r6 gauntlet re-ran `--check` and
got `1 failing` where this file said `2 failing`; every named catcher had gone
red, so the verdict was sound and only the number drifted. The runner already
requires every claimed test to go red, so "*n* claimed tests red" means *n* named
pins were measured and all *n* fired. `--verbose` prints the full failure list.

## What each mutant restores

- **`reconciler_never_started`** — Round 2's shape: delivery happens only when a notification arrives. The timer that makes the ledger the durable path is gone.
- **`reconcile_not_on_resubscribe`** — Round 2 had no listener-loss callback. With the timer still running this is a latency regression rather than a correctness one, which is exactly why it needs its own pin: every other reconciliation test stays green.
- **`head_frame_never_sent`** — Removes the unsolicited head frame. `sync` still covers rows this instance never folded; nothing covers a row it folded and broadcast whose frame one socket lost.
- **`append_execute_granted_to_public`** — Round 2's privilege block granted EXECUTE on the append function to PUBLIC, which made the call-stack trigger the guard and the door itself unlocked.
- **`append_authorizes_nobody`** — Round 2's append path performed no membership authorization at all: any caller that could reach the table wrote durable history into any room as any user. Since 0008 the rule is the core_events_invariants trigger rather than a block inside the append function, because a rule inside the function only binds callers of the function (r6 major 3).
- **`append_accepts_any_position`** — Round 2 ran no reducer validation. The reducer refuses an event for exactly two reasons and both are properties of position; without the canonical-order gate a caller writes a row a replay refuses to fold, and the server then cannot start against its own log. Now enforced on the table, so it binds a caller that never goes through the append function.
- **`append_rings_no_doorbell`** — Round 2 emitted pg_notify from the application, so a row written by anything else landed durably and told nobody. Since 0008 the emitter is an AFTER INSERT trigger rather than the append function, because a doorbell inside the function is silent for exactly the writer the comment above it names (r6 major 3).
- **`payload_may_carry_an_actor`** — Deletes the inverted r1 major 2. With #21 the payload has no actor, so the old equality became unsatisfiable and the tempting move is to drop it — taking the rule it carried with it.
- **`actor_id_may_disagree_with_kind`** — Without it, `{kind:'system', actor_id:'alice'}` is a row that reads as a person having done what the process did.
- **`server_ignores_the_page_limit`** — Collapses every catch-up to one page, which is the arrangement under which r2's suite never once ran the catch-up loop against a real database.
- **`more_is_page_fullness_across_two_reads`** — Round 1's blocking finding, whole: `more` computed from page fullness AND the page and the head read separately. Both halves are needed, and that is the point — with the snapshot read in place an untruncated page always has `to === head`, so r1's arithmetic alone produces the right answer for the wrong reason and escapes. The defect only exists when the two numbers describe two different moments.
- **`client_commits_after_applying`** — Round 2's ordering: the in-memory list moves and the durable record does not. Written as a deletion of the durable-first commit since #22 r10 put a refusal filter between the two statements — the claim is 'the journal and the cursor are written together, before the in-memory view moves', and removing the write is the sharpest way to ask whether anything checks it.
- **`client_resumes_a_cursor_without_its_events`** — Round 2's `WatermarkStore` by construction: the cursor is durable and the events are not, so a reload is a room that believes it is up to date and holds nothing.
- **`client_ignores_the_head_frame`** — Leaves a client that lost one event frame with nothing able to tell it, because its cursor and its stale head agree.
- **`client_drops_the_page_limit`** — Without a limit the client takes the server's 1000-entry default, and no fixture in this repo produces a second page.
- **`reconciler_skips_a_room_it_just_delivered`** — Round 3's inference, from the reconciler's side: a room it just fanned rows out to needs no head frame, 'because its head is announced by construction'. The fan-out is the send that may have been lost, so the room that just received rows is the one most in need of being told where it is.
- **`reconciler_passes_overlap`** — The timer, the doorbell and a resubscribe can coincide; without coalescing each opens its own pass and they queue on the ledger's in-process mutex for no benefit.
- **`reconciler_failure_escapes`** — On the timer's un-awaited call an escaping rejection is an unhandled rejection, which `index.ts` answers by exiting the process — so one bad database minute stops the durable path entirely.
- **`ledger_payload_may_carry_an_actor`** — The two ledger-only kinds never reach `CoreEvent.parse`, so without this guard they are the one door in the wall — a `message_posted` payload free to carry an actor nothing folds and nothing believes.
- **`attention_reason_reverts_to_a_sentence`** — #21 made the sentence a render of a structured reason; storing the sentence freezes today's wording into every historical row and makes 'which rule raised this' a substring search over prose.
- **`core_event_types_lose_the_sixth`** — r1 major 3, in its live form: a core type the ledger classifies as server-only is never folded and vanishes from every replay while live ingestion still applies it. Pinned by a compile-time parity assert rather than by a test — `packages/db` asserts its enum against @atrium/core's, so the divergence cannot be built, let alone shipped. Declared as `caughtBy: build` because a mutant caught by tsc has not measured any test, and a ledger that let those two look alike would print ticks for rules nothing ran.
- **`journal_forgets_the_torn_write_check`** — A partially written record is the one case where resuming is worse than replaying: the cursor names a position whose event the store does not hold, and the next since asks from past the hole. Moved into StoredRoom in r8 along with the ordering check it sat next to, because both answer the same question — is this a history — and the schema is where the two absolute sentences at the top of the file are cashed.
- **`journal_splits_into_two_keys`** — Two keys is two writes with no transaction between them — the exact window RoomJournal exists to close, reopened by the one storage API that cannot close it any other way.
- **`reconciler_latches_the_head_it_reported`** — Round 3's other half: a per-room latch that suppresses a repeat, so a socket which lost the one frame carrying a head is never told again — the head frame failing in exactly the case it exists for. The latch is hung off the callback rather than declared beside `timer` because a mutant is one substitution; the behaviour is r3's exactly.
- **`head_marked_from_fanout`** — Round 3's blocking defect, whole, expressed in r4's shape: a successful fan-out records an acknowledgement for every subscriber in the room. 'We called broadcast' becomes 'the client has it', and a socket that dropped the frame in a room that then goes quiet is never told again.
- **`head_acks_ignore_the_client`** — The other direction: never record what a client acknowledges, so the head frame is a permanent per-room heartbeat. Correct, and it makes the frame something a client learns to ignore — which is why r3 tried to suppress it in the first place.
- **`head_ack_may_go_backwards`** — Two head frames in flight are answered in whatever order the socket delivers them, so a client mid-catch-up answers the first with a cursor it has already passed. Taking the smaller number re-opens frames the client has already answered.
- **`head_acks_leak_per_connection`** — A socket that closes leaves its acknowledgements behind: one entry per connection for the life of the process, with no symptom until the memory is gone.
- **`client_never_acknowledges_the_head`** — The client half of the acknowledgement. Without it the server never learns what any socket holds and every subscribed room gets a head frame every pass, for ever.
- **`client_acknowledges_an_unfinished_catchup`** — Acknowledging a page that says `more` claims a position the client has not reached, so the server stops telling a client that is still several pages behind — the premature silence this whole finding is about, arrived at from the client side.
- **`replay_rederives_the_receipt_window`** — Round 3's blocking 2, in the shape round 5 leaves available: the replay derives the receipt window again instead of reading the row's. The derivation is the database's now and it is still a derivation *at fold time*, which is the defect — `messages.author_id` is ON DELETE SET NULL, so deleting a human author makes an acceptance that folded cleanly replay as a receipt failure. Same derivation, different substrate.
- **`append_records_no_receipt_window`** — The other end of r3's blocking 2, expressed where the derivation now lives: the boundary folds and stores no window at all. Every fold then reads NULL, which is the absence #21's reducer refuses — so a model acceptance that should land never does, live or on replay. It was a `file` mutant in r4; there is no TypeScript variable left to remove, which is the point of the round.
- **`at_spelling_unconstrained`** — Restores r2's has-a-timezone-designator check. Every spelling it admits beyond the canonical one is an instant the SQL gate treats as equal and the reducer treats as a different string, so the two disagree about whether a pair of events is simultaneous.
- **`id_charset_unconstrained`** — Without it an astral-plane id reaches the ledger, and the SQL gate's `COLLATE "C"` and the reducer's UTF-16 comparison order it differently — the canonical order stops being one order.
- **`trusted_messages_shape_unconstrained`** — The snapshot is what a replay folds a receipt against. Without the shape check a writer that is not the server can leave a window a replay cannot read, and the row that folded cleanly live becomes unfoldable.
- **`journal_grows_without_bound`** — r3's journal, unbounded. Not a slow leak: it is a guarantee of reaching the browser's quota on any room that runs long enough, and what happens at that point is the next mutant.
- **`journal_throws_on_a_full_store`** — r3's behaviour once the quota is reached: `setItem` throws, `applyEntry` leaves the cursor where it was — correctly, for a transient failure — and a full store is not transient, so the room stops advancing while the socket carries on delivering.
- **`core_id_charset_unenforced`** — The @atrium/core half of the canonical-ordering subset. Without it the application can mint an id whose UTF-16 order and whose byte order disagree, and only the database CHECK stands between that and a ledger with two orders in it.
- **`append_takes_a_caller_supplied_window`** — The r4-delta blocking finding, whole: the append boundary accepts the receipt window as a parameter and stores it. A direct caller then fabricates a well-formed snapshot and every later fold validates the receipt against the forgery. Both halves are restored, because since 0008 the derivation is the table's — an argument on the function is only reachable if the trigger also stops overwriting the column, and half of the defect is not the defect.
- **`receipt_window_ignores_the_room`** — The derivation this round replaced looked messages up by id alone, so a model acceptance in room A could be handed the text of a message from room B and check its receipt against a conversation the room never had. @atrium/core's TrustedContext doc says 'the room's own message table'; nothing enforced it.
- **`append_stores_a_window_it_did_not_derive`** — The table stores a window that is not the one the derivation produced. Nothing in SQL can notice, because both halves are the database's — so the server compares the window it folded under against the one the append reports storing, and refuses the append rather than committing a row that replays differently than it applied.
- **`payload_room_may_disagree`** — `room_id` was a lifted column nothing compared to the payload — the last of them. A direct caller files an event under room A whose payload names room B: the fan-out reads the column and delivers to A, the fold reads the payload and files it under B, and `since(A, n)` serves a row that folded into another room. Dropping the constraint outright; `payload_room_check_is_kind_blind` is the subtler half, which keeps a constraint and reverts it to the shape that could be smuggled past.
- **`id_charset_check_loses_its_collation`** — r4's charset CHECK, which spelled the range `[!-~]` with no collation. A regex bracket range is resolved in the collation of its input, so under ICU or a generated glibc locale it stops meaning printable ASCII. Invisible to every behavioural test in this suite — the compose image's en_US.utf8 behaves as byte order — which is exactly why the pin reads the deployed constraint instead.
- **`at_check_is_shape_only`** — r4's `at` CHECK: the right shape and no calendar. It admits 2026-13-45T25:00:00.000Z, which @atrium/core's Timestamp refuses — the parity the r4 delta found false, in the direction nobody had looked. Such a row then fails at the ::timestamptz cast in core_events_payload_at_matches as a cast error rather than as a named constraint.
- **`core_timestamp_accepts_any_iso`** — The other side of the same parity: @atrium/core's Timestamp stops constraining while the CHECK does not. This is r4's arrangement in miniature — a type that admits what the database refuses, so a value passes every type in the system and is refused at the INSERT.
- **`canonical_timestamp_edited_without_a_migration`** — The failure mode a shared constant introduces: the pattern moves in TypeScript and the deployed CHECK does not. Parity between the two engines still holds — they are both reading a pattern — so the fuzz stays green, and only a pin that reads pg_get_constraintdef can see that the database is enforcing last week's rule.
- **`head_acks_unbounded`** — r4's acknowledgement record: any room id a live socket names gets an entry. The cleanup on close was correct and beside the point — a socket that never closes never reaches it — so one open connection could grow the server's map without limit by acknowledging rooms it invented.
- **`journal_getitem_outside_the_try`** — r4's read path, verbatim: `getItem` outside the storage try. Browsers that refuse storage do it on access in some builds and on use in others, so a read that throws escaped `commit` — the same permanent stall the bounded-journal work was about, reached through the other half of the API while 'never throws' was on the receipt.
- **`journal_lets_the_callback_throw`** — The journal's one advertised property is that `commit` does not throw, and r4 let a caller's `onDegraded` break it — at the worst moment, since the callback only runs once something has already gone wrong.
- **`journal_degrades_silently`** — r4 made the degradation report opt-in, so a journal that had stopped being durable said nothing at all unless a caller had thought to ask. That is the failure the option exists to surface: the client keeps working, re-reads its whole history on every load, and nothing anywhere records why.
- **`receipt_window_collapses_null_into_empty`** — The derivation answers `[]` where it should answer NULL: for a human acceptance, for an event with no receipt, and for an acceptance that cites nothing. Absent and empty are different facts — #21's reducer refuses a non-human acceptance for both, and reports the two differently — so collapsing them makes a replay report the wrong reason, and gives every human acceptance a receipt window it never had.
- **`fk_delete_action_drifts`** — The failure the stale FK audit was evidence of: a delete action changes and the paragraph describing it does not. 0005's audit named a column that does not exist under an action it does not have, and omitted one that does — with no way for a reader to tell which of its other rows were also wrong. The audit is read off `pg_constraint` now, so drift fails a test instead of ageing quietly in a comment.
- **`payload_room_check_is_kind_blind`** — Round 5's version of the room check: a `coalesce` over every nested room key any member of the union might carry. It takes whichever key appears first in its list rather than the one this event kind actually uses, so an `object_accepted` filed into room B with a real `object.roomId` of room A and a smuggled `proposal: {roomId: B}` passes on the smuggled key — fan-out uses B, the fold uses A. The constraint is still there and still refuses the honest lie, which is what makes this the mutant that matters: dropping it is loud, and this is not.
- **`append_trusts_a_room_less_kind`** — The boundary stops resolving a room-less kind back to the room its subject was minted in. `proposal_rejected`, `proposal_superseded` and `object_corrected` name a proposal or an object rather than a room, so no CHECK over a single row can contradict the lifted `room_id` — a caller files a rejection of room A's proposal into room B and both the fan-out and `since(B, n)` believe it. This is r5's behaviour exactly, at r7's location.
- **`append_returns_the_window_it_meant_to_store`** — The append returns the values it *intended* rather than a `RETURNING` of the columns the table assigned — r5's body, and the overclaim in r5's receipt. The two agree today, so this changes no behaviour and **no behavioural test can catch it**; it is pinned structurally, by reading `prosrc`, and the test says so out loud. Since 0008 the same argument covers `room_seq`, which the trigger mints: a function that recomputes it is a function that can report a position the row does not hold.
- **`journal_null_store_degrades_silently`** — The fourth way the journal stops being durable, in `commit`: `storage()` answers `null` when `localStorage` is absent or throws on access, and the fallback runs without telling anybody. The room works and silently re-fetches itself from the server on every load for ever. The first version of this mutant claimed both of the tests that cover the fourth path and the ledger caught it out — `load` reported for the test that committed first, so a site with its report removed still looked measured. One mutant per site now; `journal_null_store_reads_as_no_history` is the other.
- **`journal_null_store_reads_as_no_history`** — The same silence on the read path, and the worse of the two: `readDurable` answers `{events: [], lastSeq: 0}` for a store it cannot reach. "No history" is a legitimate answer meaning "fresh room", so a client in a private-mode browser re-reads its whole history from the server on every load and nothing anywhere says why. Reachable only when `load` is the first call a room makes, which is exactly what a returning client does.
- **`inflight_recovery_is_a_no_op`** — The mutant runner’s own crash recovery stops looking. Every kill that is not a clean SIGINT then leaves an earlier round’s behaviour in the working tree — or an earlier mutant’s schema in the database — and the next run measures it and credits the results to whatever it was running at the time. The instrument having the defect it hunts, which is a standing RETRO entry.
- **`invariants_take_the_room_seq_they_are_given`** — The trigger stops minting `room_seq` and keeps whatever the INSERT supplied. The append function passes none, so every row lands NULL — but the shape that matters is the r6 exploit's, which supplied 9999: a caller-chosen position is a gap in a sequence the whole `since(room, room_seq)` contract calls contiguous.
- **`append_guard_matches_an_unqualified_name`** — r6's guard, verbatim: `position('function atrium_append_core_event(' in v_context)`. PL/pgSQL labels each stack frame with `format_procedure` at compile time, which omits the schema qualifier when that schema is on `search_path` at that moment and caches the result for the session — so a function in any schema can wear the name. The r6 gauntlet used it to file a rejection of room A's proposal into room B, at room_seq 9999, dated 2020.
- **`append_guard_opens_when_its_door_is_missing`** — The guard derives the signature it expects from the catalog, and `position(x in y)` is NULL when either side is. Written as `IF position(...) = 0` without the NULL arm, a guard whose append function has been dropped or renamed stops refusing anything at all — a fail-open guard, produced by the obvious spelling. Mutated by dropping the NULL arm and pointing the lookup at a signature that does not exist, which is the state that spelling mishandles.
- **`append_takes_no_lock`** — The append function stops taking the ledger advisory lock. This is the only way to reach the guard's *second* branch now that its first one refuses a borrowed name outright: a frame that really is the append function, without the lock. r1 shipped a hand-conversion typo in this key and every single-process test stayed green while the mutual-exclusion guarantee was simply absent.
- **`payload_room_check_does_not_fail_closed`** — The `coalesce(…, false)` wrapper is dropped from `core_events_payload_room_matches`. Both `schema.ts` and 0007 say in prose that it makes an unknown ninth kind fail closed; nothing tested it for two rounds, and it is behaviourally real — with the wrapper gone, a ninth kind with `room_id` = B and `object.roomId` = A lands, because a CHECK passes when its expression is NULL.
- **`payload_room_check_uses_equality`** — `IS NOT DISTINCT FROM` becomes `=` in the second clause. This changes no behaviour — clause 1 already guarantees the declared key is present and non-NULL, and `ELSE room_id::text` covers the rest, so no input separates the two spellings; the round-7 comments say exactly that instead of the justification they used to give. It is in the ledger to keep the structural pin honest: a corrected comment with nothing holding the code to it is the same defect one round later.
- **`event_type_drifts_from_the_deployed_enum`** — The drizzle event_type enum grows a value the database does not have. _CoreEventTypeCoverage asserts only that every core event type is in the enum, so this compiles. It pins that a comparison exists at all — and it is honest to say it does not discriminate r7 from r6, because r6 compared Object.keys(OWN_KEY) against eventType.enumValues and this trips that too. The direction r7 added is the database growing a kind TypeScript has not heard of, which cannot be a mutant at all: ALTER TYPE ... ADD VALUE is irreversible, so it would leak a ninth kind into every later file in the run. That half is verified by hand and the test says so.
- **`bus_relays_whatever_is_published`** — The ephemeral channel goes back to casting: `JSON.parse(raw) as EphemeralAnnouncement`, which is r6 exactly. `NOTIFY` needs no privilege, so anything that can reach the database publishes a frame and `hub.broadcast` fans it out — including a durable `event` frame, which the client commits to its journal and advances `lastSeq` past, permanently skipping the real event at that position.
- **`client_casts_the_frame_it_was_sent`** — The client goes back to `JSON.parse(String(event.data)) as ServerFrame`. `handleFrame` reaches `applyEntry`, which writes the durable journal and moves `lastSeq`, so a frame accepted on the strength of a cast is a position the real event can never occupy — the durable half of r6's major 1.
- **`journal_casts_what_it_reads_back`** — The journal goes back to `parsed.events as RoomEventEnvelope[]` behind two `typeof` checks. `localStorage` is shared with everything else on the origin and survives reloads, so a poisoned record is a `lastSeq` this client resumes from — and every real event at or below it is silently skipped. It was the last cast on a durable path in the client.
- **`client_resumes_a_cursor_past_the_head`** — The client stops checking its resumed cursor against the head the server states in the subscribed reply. Parsing the journal makes it well-formed, not authentic — localStorage is same-origin and carries no provenance — so a well-shaped forgery with lastSeq 50 resumes a room at 50 and skips every real position at or below it, permanently. Both foreign-lineage reviewers found this in r7s first draft; the arithmetic is the only check available, because the head is the one number the client did not write.
- **`client_lets_an_event_body_carry_an_actor`** — The client stops refusing an actor inside an event body. z.looseObject keeps unknown keys, so without this refinement event.actor survives the parse while the comment beside it says there is no such field — which is what a foreign-lineage probe of r7s first draft got back out of the journal. The server refuses a payload actor three times over, so a body carrying one did not come from the ledger.
- **`client_applies_a_catchup_page_for_another_room`** — The client stops requiring a catch-up page entries to name the page room. handleFrame does its arithmetic against view(frame.roomId) while applyEntry files each entry under entry.roomId, so a page whose entries name another room moves one room journal on another room cursor. The same cross-check exists on the bus (EphemeralNote) and was missing on the socket — an asymmetry inside r7 own fix, found by a second lineage.
- **`journal_forgets_the_ordering_check`** — r7's schema checked the record against its own cursor and never against itself, which is #22 gauntlet r7 defect 2. {events:[{roomSeq:9},{roomSeq:2}], lastSeq:2} is self-consistent by that rule and is not a history: the 9 is in the timeline while the cursor is 2, applyEntry dedups on roomSeq <= lastSeq, and the real event at 9 arrives in catch-up and is applied a second time. The room renders [9,2,3,4,5,6,7,8,9] under a file whose first paragraph says nothing is ever applied out of order and nothing is applied twice.
- **`journal_reads_another_rooms_events`** — The same question the ordering check answers, asked of the other field the record carries: roomId. The key names the room; the envelopes carry their own, and view() renders held.events as this room's timeline without re-reading them. An entry filed under room A carrying room B's roomId is cross-room content injection for the cost of one setItem, from a store the origin shares with everything on it.
- **`journal_reset_leaves_the_record_on_disk`** — #22 gauntlet r7 defect 3. reset promises 'after it returns, this room resumes from nothing', and r7 answered a throwing removeItem by degrading — true for the live instance, false for the store. The poisoned key survived, so the next page load built a fresh journal with an empty degraded set, read the forgery again, fired the same check again, and degraded again, for ever. Resuming is what happens after a reload, so a degradation cannot be the whole of it.
- **`guard_stops_saying_what_it_is`** — #22 gauntlet r7 defect 1 was a SENTENCE, not a statement: the migration claimed the remaining bypass of core_events_append_guard 'costs CREATE on schema public', and it costs one SQL comment from a bare DO block. The code is unchanged in r8 on purpose — no substring over caller-authored text can be a boundary — so the only thing standing between a reader and that belief is the description. A claim with nothing testing it is exactly what this defect was, so the claim is what this mutant removes.
- **`the_socket_chooses_the_proposer`** — #22 r9 D1, the command-layer half. draftToProposal mints the proposer from the session; this makes it a passthrough of whatever the caller named, which is r8's model branch generalized to both spellings. ProposalDraft no longer carries the field, so the mutated code reads a key zod strips and the proposal reaches the ledger with no proposer at all — CoreEvent.parse refuses it, and the tests that assert a socket-staged proposal is filed under the session and accepted into an object stop passing. Recorded honestly: a faithful reintroduction of r8's behaviour needs the schema field back as well, which is a second site and is not expressible in one substitution. What this pins is that the derivation exists at all and is not read from the draft.
- **`the_stager_is_whatever_the_reading_claims`** — #22 r9 D1. ProposalRecord.stagedBy is minted from the trusted actor; this reads it off the proposal's own proposer instead whenever the proposal claims a model, which is the caller's field. It is the exact shape of the defect one layer up — ask what the guard's input is made of and who wrote it — because selfStagedReadingRefusal compares stagedBy against the accepting actor, and a stagedBy read off a model proposer is never a human and never matches. The machine-dressed forgery goes through again with the refusal still sitting in the source. (The human-proposer clause still fires under this mutation, which is why it claims only the model test: a mutant scored on a test it does not actually break is the vacuity this ledger exists to rule out.)
- **`a_human_acceptance_is_always_the_receipt`** — #22 r9 D1, the rule that closes the class. Computes the self-staged refusal and throws the answer away, which restores r8 exactly: a human matches every proposer through actorMatchesProposer, a human acceptance runs none of the receipt gates and is itself the third-party confirmation, so the person who wrote a sentence accepts it himself and mints durable state on his own word — a model attribution nobody is answerable for, or a commitment against a colleague, or both. Written as a discarded call rather than a deletion on purpose: a rule that is computed and not acted on is the shape this repo keeps finding (a check that is a manner rather than a boundary), and it is the shape a deletion would not test, because deleting the block leaves the import unused and tsc catches it instead of a test.
- **`the_read_model_repeats_the_marking_the_stager_chose`** — #22 r9 D1, fact 3. The proposals projection writes staged_by_* from the reducer's trusted record; this writes it from the proposal's own proposer instead, which is what the read model held before r9 — proposer_kind and proposer_model and nothing that could name the person who typed them. The core refusal still fires, so nothing is minted; every query over the read model is nonetheless back to repeating the marking the attacker chose. Claims only the model-proposal test: for a socket-staged proposal the proposer IS the session, so the two derivations agree and a test over that path cannot tell them apart — which is exactly why the case that matters had to be driven through a model-attributed proposal.
- **`the_fan_out_set_is_never_rechecked`** — #22 r9 D2. Makes the revalidation pass return before it looks at anything, which is r8's shipped behaviour exactly: the hub holds a subscription until the socket closes, broadcast consults that map and not memberships, and a revoked member keeps receiving the room's event frames with full message bodies and its head frames until they disconnect — which the shipped client does not do voluntarily and undoes by reconnecting. The bound was not a duration; this restores it to not being one.
- **`the_revocation_pass_never_runs_on_its_own`** — #22 r9 D2, the other half: the rule can be perfect and unreached. Removes the body of the timer that drives it, so revalidateSubscriptions is only ever called by a test calling it directly — which is precisely the arrangement that would let this ship green while a revoked member reads the room forever, because every integration test above drives the pass by hand on purpose. The window it names stops being a window.
- **`the_attribution_gate_is_per_verb_again`** — #22 r10's organizing defect. Removes the gate from the one place every correction verb passes through, leaving the pre-r10 arrangement where the only thing standing between a member and a colleague's name was the `amend`/`reattribute` verb split — which `reattribute` and `retype` both walk around by definition. Written as a deletion of the choke-point call rather than as a narrowed condition, because the claim being tested is structural: `commitPlan` is the only writer of `record.object`, and the gate runs immediately before it, so no verb can reach state without it. Written as a discarded call rather than a deletion, and the first full pass is why: deleting it leaves `correctionAttributionRefusal` unused, `tsc` refuses the build, and the runner reports ERROR because the compiler caught the mutant and no test was ever asked. A rule that is computed and not acted on is also the shape this repo keeps finding. Since r11 the call passes the two objects rather than two name arrays, so this also discards the sentence half of the gate.
- **`the_gate_refuses_a_name_that_was_already_there`** — The other direction, and the one a fix for r10's D1 is most likely to get wrong: the rule is about a name *arriving*, not a name being present. Tell the gate the object named nobody a moment ago and every amend, retract and restore on somebody else's commitment is refused — the product freezes rather than leaks, which is a different bug and just as shipped. Mutated inside the predicate since r11: the call site now passes the object, not the name set, and blanking `before` there would also blind the sentence clause — two rules broken by one substitution measures neither. `before` stays in use by `objectStatement`, so `tsc` has nothing to say and a test is still what notices.
- **`the_gate_never_refuses_on_the_sentence`** — #22 r11's defect, restored. The gate compares name sets and never acts on the text, which is the state r10 shipped — and its refusal string went on citing *nobody gets committed, **or quoted**, by someone else's sentence* while enforcing only the first half. With this in place a member takes a colleague's own accepted commitment and rewrites the words under his name, five commands, `ack` with `issues: []` every time, ending at a verified claim in which the colleague confesses to taking kickbacks. Written as `|| true` on the early return rather than as a deletion of the clause, so both `objectStatement` calls stay referenced and the compiler has no opinion: the claim is that a *test* notices, and under r10 none did.
- **`the_gate_never_refuses_on_the_sentence_over_the_wire`** — The same substitution as `the_gate_never_refuses_on_the_sentence`, measured against a real server, a real Postgres and three real sockets. It is not redundant with its unit twin: the unit suite folds a log, and what r10's D4 established is that a refusal reaching the actor's `ack` and a refusal reaching the room are different facts. This is the one that fails if the gate is right in the reducer and the room is told nothing — and the one that fails if `accepted_objects` is written by a path the fold does not gate.
- **`the_sentence_clause_fires_on_a_name_being_present`** — The too-strong version of r11, and the one a naive fix lands on: refuse whenever the object bears somebody else's name, rather than when the sentence under it changes. `retract`, `restore`, `reopen`, `amend` of a due date and `amend` of a status all stop working on anybody else's object — r10 made that its own named mutant for the name clause, and the sentence clause needs the same pin or the product freezes instead of leaking. Written as `&& false` so the comparison stays type-checked and only its effect is removed.
- **`the_sentence_clause_ignores_whose_name_it_is`** — The same over-reach one clause down: the sentence may only be reworded by the person it names, and dropping the `isForeign` filter makes it rewordable by nobody at all. A person could no longer fix the wording of their own commitment, and a model's reading of somebody's words could never be refined by that person — which is the one correction the product most needs to keep, because it is what turns `~` into `✓`.
- **`the_text_field_is_hand_written_again`** — r10 found three hand-written answers to *which field names a person* where the brief said two. `payloadText` was the same defect one field over — a ladder spelling out `open_question ? 'question' : objective ? 'title' : 'statement'` beside the `TEXT_FIELD` that `attribution.ts` derives from `PAYLOAD_FIELD_ROLE`, two answers to *which field holds the sentence*, agreeing today and free to disagree the day a sixth type arrives. r11 made the derivation the only answer; this restores the ladder with one arm wrong, which is exactly how the two would come apart in practice. Nothing about an objective's text is right afterwards: it cannot be quoted, retyped away from, or receipted. The `void TEXT_FIELD` is not decoration — without it the import goes unused, `tsc` refuses the build, and the compiler rather than a test is what caught the mutant.
- **`a_decision_names_nobody`** — #22 r10, D2, at its root. `authority.ts` asserted in prose that 'a decision, an objective and an open question name nobody', `payloadAttributedTo` implemented that sentence, and `DecisionPayload.decidedBy` contradicted both. Reclassifying the field is the smallest way to restore the disagreement: the table still exists, the gates still run, and the room's record can still say the victim cancelled the audit.
- **`the_mint_gate_is_inside_the_proposal_block_again`** — The fifth route, which #22 r10's brief did not name and the matrix listed as *allowed*: an acceptance citing no proposal has no stager but the accepter, so it is the self-staged shape with the second party removed rather than merely absent — and r9's gate lived inside `if (proposalId !== null)`. Human-only, unreachable from today's command layer, and reachable by design the moment anything mints a fact outright. Skips the gate when there is no proposal, exactly as r9 did.
- **`retype_leaves_the_read_model_behind`** — #22 r10, D3's read-model half. `projectObjectCorrected` wrote payload, revision, retracted/superseded and updatedAt and never `type`, which was only ever written at insert — so a `retype` left the row permanently disagreeing with the fold about what the object is, with both partial indexes on `(room_id, type)` filing it under the type it used to be. Proven across a restart: the fold said commitment and the row said objective, and nothing reconverged them. Filed wider as #56; this is the field a verb in this event's own vocabulary changes.
- **`a_refused_row_is_broadcast_unmarked`** — #22 r10, D4. The refusal convention delivers `issues` to the actor's own socket and to nobody else, while the row — refused, changing nothing — is appended and fanned out in full to every subscriber and replayed to cold readers by `since`. Strips the marker from the wire converter, which is the catch-up path *and* the reconciler's fan-out; the live command path keeps its own, so a test that only watched a live broadcast would still pass. Note what it does *not* reach: `catchUpPage` is the ledger's own method and the multi-instance test calls it directly, so that test is `foldThrough`'s and not this one's — the wire converter is the last step before the socket, and only a test that reads a socket sees it.
- **`catch_up_answers_about_rows_it_has_not_folded`** — The fail-open inside #22 r10's D4 fix. `issuesFor` reads `CoreState.issues`, so 'this row recorded no issue' and 'this instance has not folded this row' are the same answer unless the read path folds first. Removing the fold makes every row another instance committed come back marked clean — silently, and only for the multi-instance case, which is the shape that survives a single- instance test suite.
- **`the_client_shows_a_row_the_server_refused`** — #22 r10, D4's client half. A refused row is not an event that happened, and the room's materialised history must not contain a sentence the server refused — but the cursor must still advance past it, because `room_seq` is gap-free and the journal's record requires its cursor to name the entry it holds. Puts the row back in `room.events`, which is where r9 left it: in every subscriber's timeline and in their durable journal, across a reload.
